The interrogation room had one light, and it was doing the bare minimum.

Detective Rusk sat under it with his sleeves rolled up, smoking a cigarette that smelled like it had been swept off a factory floor. Detective Bell stood behind me with the phone book. Every time I gave Rusk an answer he didn’t like, Bell looked up my number.

“Where’s the ledger?” Rusk asked.

“I thought you boys came down here to report a crime.”

The phone book hit me. For a second there was no room, no light, no Rusk. Just pain, bright and stupid, taking up all the space in my head. Then the room came back, and with it the smell of cheap tobacco. My old man used to smoke the same brand at the kitchen table while he counted out the rent. I hadn’t thought of him in years. I resented Rusk for bringing him into it.

“Won’t leave a bruise,” Bell said.

“You want a medal or a patent?”

Bell shifted his grip. Rusk raised a finger, and Bell stopped. That was interesting. I’d always figured Bell for the senior partner. He certainly ate like one.

Rusk tapped his ash into a paper cup. “A woman named Evelyn Shaw came to your office at four this afternoon. She left at four-twenty. We know what she brought you.”

“Then I don’t see why you’re keeping me up.”

“She tell you where she got it?”

“No.”

That was the truth. Evelyn had set the ledger on my desk and asked what it would cost to get her brother out of town. I’d told her to bring him in so we could talk. She said he’d been dead since Tuesday. Then she asked me again.

Bell’s shoes creaked behind me. I caught myself waiting for the next hit and hated that worse than the pain. At least the pain had the decency to happen all at once.

Rusk leaned forward. “You want to walk out of here tonight?”

“Sure.”

“Then give me something.”

“All right,” I said. “Which one of you signed for the body?”

Rusk’s cigarette stopped halfway to his mouth.

Behind me, Bell set the phone book down. Not gently. Not like a man who was finished with it, either.

Then he said, “You told me there wasn’t a body.”

For the first time all night, neither of them was looking at me. I took a breath. It hurt clear down to my belt, but it was mine, and nobody interrupted it.

The starter dropped her hand, and the whole underpass turned white.

Headlights swept the concrete pillars. Tires screamed. Mara caught the smell of burning rubber through her open window, hot and bitter, with raw gasoline underneath it. Two hundred people had packed themselves behind the columns to watch. In her mirror, they vanished in the smoke before she’d even hit third.

At the far end of the service road, a floodlight marked the hairpin. Brake there, turn hard, come back under the bridge. She’d walked it twice that afternoon, counting the paces from the light to the barrier.

The black coupe alongside her was half a hood ahead. Its driver looked over. She saw his teeth.

Mara held on for one more second.

Then she braked.

The pedal went to the floor.

She lifted her foot and stamped again. Nothing. Her seat belt hung loose across her chest; her body had braced for a force that never came.

The coupe’s brake lights flared. It dropped behind her so fast it seemed to go backward.

The first thing the prison gave Mara was a toothache.

It throbbed in a molar she had never had, on the left side of a mouth that tasted faintly of coffee. Her tongue went to it with the practiced irritation of someone who had been doing this all week.

Then she saw the red sleeve.

At her trial, the sleeve had stuck out from beneath a silver blanket. The prosecutor had put the photograph on a screen large enough that Mara could see individual loops of wool.

Now the sleeve was on her arm.

“Four minutes and twelve seconds,” said the clinician, somewhere beyond the memory. “You may find it helpful not to count.”

The woman whose body Mara occupied was carrying groceries up three flights of stairs. On the second landing she stopped to move the eggs to the top of the bag. She was thinking that the dentist would ask whether she’d been flossing and that, for once, she would say no. She was tired of lying to a man who knew perfectly well.

Her name was Elise Venn. Mara had known that for eleven years. She had not known about the tooth.

At the top of the stairs, Elise saw that her apartment door was open.

She stopped walking, but the groceries swung forward and bumped her knee. For a moment she thought her son had come home early. The relief of it was so quick and so ordinary that Mara felt herself reach for it too.

Then came the sound of a drawer shutting.

Mara had been looking for cash. She remembered closing that drawer with her hip. She remembered being annoyed because it kept sliding open.

*Go downstairs*, she thought.

Elise called her son’s name.

What frightened Mara most, afterward, was how long Elise went on expecting to live. Even when Mara stepped into the hall, Elise believed there was something she could say that would get them both out of this. She set the groceries down carefully, the way you set something down when you don’t want to startle a dog. She said there was money in the blue bowl by the door. She said it twice because the first time her voice barely came out.

Then she saw Mara’s face.

Mara remembered what she had been thinking in that instant: *She can identify me.*

From the other side, it wasn’t a thought. It was a small, awful change in a stranger’s expression, and Elise understood it before she could explain it to herself. Her body tried to back away. Her heel caught the grocery bag. An orange rolled out.

For eleven years Mara had remembered the orange.

She hadn’t remembered that the woman had said *please* until she felt the word form against the sore tooth.

At the end, Elise thought of her son’s key. He had lost it twice that winter. She had sewn a little pocket inside his schoolbag and made him show her that morning that he knew where it was. Now she wanted, with a force that seemed too much for one body, to go back to the kitchen and take it from him. If he didn’t have his key, he would knock. If no one answered, he might go next door. He might not have to come in and see.

She tried to hold on to the picture of him standing safely on the landing, getting impatient, knocking again.

Then she couldn’t hold even that.

The ceiling of the prison came back one white tile at a time. The clinician loosened the straps. Mara turned her head and was sick into a basin someone had already put beside the chair.

“Can you state what you’ve learned?” he asked.

She knew the answer he wanted. It was printed on the wall across from her bed. She had seen men come back from this room saying it over and over, getting the wording right before their hands had stopped shaking.

“Does her son know you do this?” Mara asked.

The clinician looked down at his tablet. For a moment she thought he was checking. Then his thumb moved, and she heard the click of the straps resetting for another session.

Mara lay very still. In a moment she would be on the stairs again. The tooth would hurt, the coffee would be bitter, and for a little while Elise would still have nothing worse to worry about than what to say to the dentist.

Mara wanted those seconds back so badly that she understood, at last, how little they belonged to her.

For the last mile, something in the woods had been matching Nora’s pace.

When she stopped, it stopped. When she scuffed a boot through the leaves, she heard an answering scuff among the trees. Once, she’d taken two quick steps and then a slow one, just to see.

Two quick. One slow.

The old footbridge came into view below her. A man stood at the near end of it, barefoot in the frost. He wore a flannel shirt she recognized before she recognized his face.

“Mr. Voss?”

He’d sharpened her skates every winter since she was six. There was a little burn on his cuff where he’d leaned against the stove in his shop. She found herself looking at that burn while his knees broke.

The first crack made her take a step toward him. It was instinct: someone had fallen, someone needed help. Then came a second crack, and he rose without straightening. His heels lifted. The bones in his feet lengthened under the skin, pushing his toes apart on the boards.

“Nora,” he said.

Her name came out almost right.

He caught hold of the bridge rail. The knuckles swelled one after another, and the skin between them went pale and shiny as it stretched. A seam gave way at his shoulder. Under the torn flannel, his spine lifted in a series of hard little jerks, each with its own sound. Nora could hear him trying to breathe between them.

He looked up at her. For one absurd second she thought he was about to sneeze. His upper lip drew back, his eyes squeezed shut, and then his jaw broke with a noise like a cup dropped on a kitchen floor. His face pushed forward. The skin pulled so tight along his cheeks that she could see the roots of his teeth through it.

Nora backed away. A twig snapped under her boot.

The thing on the bridge cocked its head. Then it stepped down onto a twig of its own, with a small, deliberate crunch.

She understood, finally, that it had never been trying to follow her quietly.

By midnight, the bite had stopped bleeding. This seemed unfair to Ruth. Something that was going to kill her brother ought to look worse than it did.

Eli sat against the laundromat wall with his bad arm in his lap. Every few minutes he tried to pull his sleeve down over the bite. The cuff would catch, and he would forget why he’d wanted to cover it in the first place.

“We could wait until morning,” Ruth said.

Nessa looked toward the back room, where the children were sleeping between the dryers. “If we wait, we have to put him somewhere he can’t get out.”

“The stockroom has a lock.”

“It does,” Nessa said.

They’d locked Mr. Vale in a stockroom. He’d called for his wife long after he’d stopped sounding like himself. None of them knew whether that meant he was still in there.

Eli lifted his head. “I don’t want the stockroom.”

Ruth crouched beside him. “I could sit outside the door.”

“I know. I’d hear you.”

She waited for him to say that would help. After a moment she understood it was the reason he didn’t want her there.

Across the room, Cal set his mug down carefully. He’d been holding it with both hands since they brought Eli in, though there was nothing in it.

“I can do it,” he said.

Ruth looked up at him. Last week he’d dropped an entire jar of peaches and stood barefoot among the pieces, apologizing to each of them in turn. She couldn’t bear that he was offering. She couldn’t bear the thought that he might take it back.

“Nessa?” Eli said.

Nessa knelt and felt his forehead. It was an old habit from when she’d had a thermometer, when a fever was a thing you took a number for. “I don’t think you have until morning,” she said.

“All right.” He swallowed. “Cal, then.”

Ruth gripped his good hand hard enough that he winced.

“Sorry,” she said, and let go.

“No, keep it.”

So she took his hand again. Nessa went to sit with the children. Cal waited by the row of washers while Ruth tried to think of something she hadn’t already told her brother. She’d spent the last six months telling him to tie his boots properly and drink more water and stop going ahead of her around corners.

“Remember when you called me from the bus station?” she said.

“Which time?”

She laughed. There had been three times. Once he’d had money for the fare home and just hadn’t wanted to ride alone.

“I liked coming to get you,” she said. “I know I complained.”

“You complained the whole way home.”

“Yeah.”

His thumb moved against hers. “I knew.”

Cal came over. Eli shut his eyes, then opened them again to look at Ruth. She kept her face where he could see it.

Afterward, Cal said her name. She told him to wait. There was nothing she needed him to wait for, but he did.

Eli’s hand was still warm. For a little while that made it possible to sit beside him without understanding. Then Ruth’s foot began to go numb. She shifted, and his hand slipped out of hers. She caught it before it struck the tile and laid it gently in his lap.

His sleeve had ridden up again. This time she got the cuff all the way down.

She waited for him to say that would help. After a moment she understood it was the reason he didn’t want her there.

Across the room, Cal set his mug down carefully. He’d been holding it with both hands since they brought Eli in, though there was nothing in it.

“I can do it,” he said.

Ruth looked up at him. Last week he’d dropped an entire jar of peaches and stood barefoot among the pieces, apologizing to each of them in turn. She couldn’t bear that he was offering. She couldn’t bear the thought that he might take it back.

“Nessa?” Eli said.

Nessa knelt and felt his forehead. It was an old habit from when she’d had a thermometer, when a fever was a thing you took a number for. “I don’t think you have until morning,” she said.

“All right.” He swallowed. “Cal, then.”

Ruth gripped his good hand hard enough that he winced.

“Sorry,” she said, and let go.

“No, keep it.”

So she took his hand again. Nessa went to sit with the children. Cal waited by the row of washers while Ruth tried to think of something she hadn’t already told her brother. She’d spent the last six months telling him to tie his boots properly and drink more water and stop going ahead of her around corners.

“Remember when you called me from the bus station?” she said.

“Which time?”

“I liked coming to get you,” she said. “I know I complained.”

“Yeah.”

His thumb moved against hers. “I knew.”

Cal came over. Eli shut his eyes, then opened them again to look at Ruth. She kept her face where he could see it.

For the first week, what frightened him was how well he slept.

He had expected to lie awake rehearsing the murder. Instead he slept eight hours, woke hungry, and stood at the stove wondering whether the eggs were still good. On Thursday he laughed at something a cashier said. Halfway home he stopped with the grocery bag cutting into his fingers, trying to remember the joke. It seemed important that he should be able to remember what had made him laugh.

The first time he saw her, she was standing at the far end of the cereal aisle. He caught the green of her coat and the small, impatient lift of one shoulder. He turned, already stepping aside to let her pass. There was nobody there. He bought the wrong cereal and ate it every morning for a month because going back down that aisle would have meant admitting he’d been avoiding it.

After that she appeared mostly when he was doing something with his hands. Washing a knife. Untangling a cord. Trying to get a key off its ring. The moment he looked, she was gone. He learned to finish what he was doing without looking up. Then he learned to do it badly, in a hurry, so he could leave the room. By winter there were half-washed cups in every room of the apartment.

The worst of it was how ordinary his excuses sounded. He told his sister he wasn’t coming to dinner because he’d fallen behind on the laundry. It was true; he’d worn the same shirt for six days. When she offered to come over and put a load in, he told her he’d already started one. He spent the next forty minutes on the phone making sure she believed him. Afterward he couldn’t remember a single thing she’d said about her own life.

Then his memory of the murder began to change. He had always remembered her saying his name. Now some nights she said *wait*. Other nights she was trying to tell him something and he kept interrupting, the way he used to when she took too long to get to the point. He wanted the first version back. It had been awful, but at least he had known which parts of it belonged to him.

Months later, he saw her by the kitchen window as the kettle came to a boil. For once he didn’t turn. He took down two cups and asked if she still took milk.

He waited. The kettle clicked off.

“You could’ve just said no,” he muttered, and put the second cup away a little too hard. The small flare of irritation was so familiar that for a moment he forgot she was dead. Then he stood with his hand on the cupboard door, ashamed of how badly he wanted that moment back.

The strange thing was that he could still hear the radiator ticking.

He had drowned once before, briefly, at a quarry when he was nine. There had been green light and the pale soles of his brother’s feet above him. He had known which way to go. Here there was no *up*. There was a room, and somewhere in it a radiator, and the knowledge that he was on dry land was of no use to him at all.

“Where did your unit cross?”

He meant to say he didn’t know. He had been saying it all morning. But his body took the small breath he’d saved for the words and spent it trying not to die.

Then he could breathe.

He sucked in air so fast it hurt. Before he’d even finished coughing, he said, “Wait.” He hadn’t decided to say it. The word came out in the tone he used when he needed someone to hold a door.

The man asking the questions waited.

That was worse, for a moment, than if he hadn’t. The prisoner could hear his own breath slowing. His body was already taking the quiet for a promise, and he knew better, and he couldn’t make himself stop hoping.

“Where did your unit cross?”

He fixed his eyes on a little chip in the wall. The plaster underneath was pink. He thought of telling them about the quarry. There was a road down to it, and a gate his brother used to climb. It was four hundred miles away. He could give them every turn.

His mouth was open. He shut it.

The radiator ticked again. He had been counting the ticks, once. He couldn’t remember when he’d stopped.

The last train out of the city was already moving when Nera Vale dropped onto its roof.

Through the glass she saw her quarry, Ivo Sen, sitting alone in a first-class carriage with a paper suitcase on his knees. Paper was expensive enough that she wondered what he’d put in it. Then he looked up, saw her shadow, and wedged the suitcase under his seat before he ran.

Nera came through the service hatch. “Ivo. The warrant says alive. I’d like to keep it that simple.”

He tore an emergency hammer from its bracket and swung. Nera ducked the first blow. The second glanced off her shoulder, numbing her arm to the fingertips. She drew her stun weapon with the other hand.

The discharge cracked louder than she remembered.

Ivo’s muscles seized. His back arched and his jaw clenched so hard she heard his teeth click. He didn’t fly backward like people did in the serials. His knees just stopped holding him. He struck the aisle shoulder-first, his hand still knotted around the hammer. When the current cut out, his fingers opened one at a time.

For a beat he didn’t breathe. Then he dragged in a ragged breath and tried to lift his head.

“Stay down,” Nera said, kneeling beside him.

“I’m trying,” he whispered. His legs were still trembling.

She pushed the hammer out of reach and pressed two fingers to his neck. His pulse was fast, with an uneven beat she didn’t like.

“Dispatch, I have Sen. Send a medic to the next stop.”

“Is that necessary?” Ivo asked.

“You tell me. What stop did we just pass?”

His eyes went to the dark window. He opened his mouth, then shut it again.

Nera cuffed him and fetched the suitcase. One corner had split in the struggle. Inside was a stack of cheap exercise books, each with a child’s name on the cover.

“They closed the school while we were in class,” Ivo said. “I told the kids I’d mark their work.”

Nera looked at the warrant glowing on her wrist. The charge was theft of municipal property. The property wasn’t specified.

As the train slowed, she took a strip of evidence tape from her coat and used it to mend the corner of the suitcase.

Nora woke with her cheek on a tile grout line. She could see, at floor level, a little crescent of dirt the mop had missed. For a few seconds she thought she was at work, that she’d fainted in the staff bathroom again and someone would come in and be kind about it.

Then she tried to lift her head. The cuff around her wrist caught.

The instructions were printed on a laminated sheet. Whoever had put it there had rounded the corners.

The key was out of reach. She could get to it if she hurt herself. The sheet was quite plain about that, though it used the word *choose* three times, as if repetition might make it true.

She tugged at the cuff until it hurt, then stopped. She sat with that small hurt, waiting for it to tell her something useful about the larger one. All it told her was that she didn’t want any more.

Above the door, the timer changed from 01:00 to 00:59.

She rolled up her sleeve. The first fold slipped down. She made it again, tighter this time, with the neatness she used to roll her father’s sleeves before he washed the dishes. He’d call her on Sunday. If she didn’t pick up, he’d assume she was asleep and call again at noon. He was very good about letting her sleep.

“No,” she said aloud.

She hadn’t meant to say it. But it felt important to have said it at least once in this room.

She planted both heels on the tile and shifted until her back rested against the wall. Her free hand shook so badly she had to set it down twice before it stayed where she put it.

She’d been waiting to feel ready. At thirty seconds she understood that she could spend the rest of her life waiting, and that in this room the rest of her life was a very short time.

She took one more breath. It didn’t steady her. She went ahead shaking.

The plank dipped under Mara’s bare feet.

“Another step,” said Captain Vale.

She could hear him behind her, though she’d stopped looking back. The last time she’d turned, she’d caught Ned studying a knot in the deck. Two nights ago he’d sworn he would follow her anywhere. Now she wanted him to look up for just a second. She didn’t even need him to say anything.

Below, the sharks circled in the ship’s shadow. One passed close enough that she saw the pale seam of an old scar along its back. Farther out, a fin broke the surface, turned, and came in again. She tried counting them until she realized she couldn’t tell which ones she’d counted already.

The ship rolled. Her knees bent of their own accord, and someone on deck sucked in a breath. Such a small, familiar sound. She’d heard it a hundred times when a cup slid toward the edge of a table.

“I can swim,” she said.

She hadn’t meant to speak. As a girl she’d swum across the harbor on a dare and come home with her dress stuck to her legs, laughing too hard to explain herself. She tried to remember what she’d done with her hands. Suddenly it seemed important to know.

The tip of the plank rose. Beneath it, the scarred shark turned, showing a flash of white.

Behind her, Ned said her name.

Mara looked back. He was looking at her at last. She opened her mouth to tell him not to watch, but the plank dipped again, and this time her feet slipped.

“Goddamn it,” she said.

She stood up.

She always left it horizontal.

An attendant brought out the flour in a white paper sack. He asked Mara to hold it higher for the cameras. As she took it, she saw a name on the label that wasn’t hers.

“Wrong one,” she said.

The attendant peeled the label off. Underneath was another.

“That’s yours,” he said.

She found the dead man’s family in the front row because they were the only ones still sitting. There were three of them. The smallest was clapping, a little out of time with the rest of the crowd. The woman beside him reached over and held his hands.

The night Ellis tampered with Martin Vale’s brakes, he came home and washed two mugs. One was his. The other had been his daughter’s. He still took it down from the cupboard sometimes without thinking.

At the trial, Martin had said he looked at his phone for only a second. Ellis had spent four years imagining that second. Sometimes he imagined the message was important. That was worse, somehow, than imagining it was nothing.

He told himself he hadn’t decided to kill Martin. He’d only arranged for Martin to press his foot down and find out what Sophie had known in the last second of her life: that something she counted on wasn’t going to work. If Martin survived, that would be enough.

Ellis had rehearsed this distinction until it sounded like one.

At seven the next morning, he watched from his kitchen as Martin came out with a travel mug. Then Martin’s front door opened again, and his little boy ran down the steps, one shoe untied. Martin put the mug on the roof of the car and knelt to tie it.

Ellis had known about the boy. He’d watched him learn to ride a bike. Yet in all his careful thinking about the morning, he had pictured Martin getting into the car alone.

He called Martin. Across the street, Martin took his phone out, glanced at the screen, and put it back in his pocket.

Ellis ran outside in his socks.

“Don’t start the car,” he shouted.

Martin looked up. He was still holding the boy’s shoelace.

“What did you do?” he asked.

Ellis had prepared an answer to that, too. He’d meant to say, *The same thing you did.*

But Martin hadn’t gone out the night before and come home and washed two mugs.

“I tried to kill you,” Ellis said. “Get him away from the car.”

It hit her hard enough to put her on her back. Her elbow cracked against the curb. The bread rolled into the gutter, and they both went for it. She got there first. The dog closed its teeth around her sleeve and shook until she felt the cloth tear and something underneath it tear too.

She screamed. The dog didn’t let go. Its ribs jerked against her knee, each one distinct through the filthy coat. It was as thin as she was. That ought to have made her feel something. All she could think was that if she opened her hand, the bread would be gone.

They thrashed in the gutter until her boot caught the dog somewhere soft. It let go with a high, startled yelp. Then it stood a few feet away, one forepaw lifted, watching her fist.

Mara shoved the bread into her mouth. It tasted of rainwater and mold, and she swallowed before she’d chewed it enough. A lump stuck in her throat. For one stupid, bewildered second she thought she might choke to death on it.

Then it went down.

The dog was still watching. Mara licked the wet crumbs from the crease of her palm, and her stomach cramped as if she hadn’t eaten at all.

“Give me the whiskey,” Ellis said.

Mara held the bottle to his mouth. Its neck clicked against his teeth. He managed one swallow before he turned his head and coughed amber spit down his chin.

“That’s enough,” he said, though she hadn’t taken it away yet.

The shooting had stopped a minute ago. In the quiet, Mara could hear water dripping from the pump house roof and the small, wet sound Ellis’s wound made whenever he shifted. The bullet had struck high in his thigh. His trousers were black from the hip to the knee.

“Tell me when you’re going to do it,” he said.

She opened the knife.

“No,” he said. “I changed my mind. Don’t tell me.”

The first cut made a sound she’d remember long after she forgot the sound of the gun: a faint rasp, like a dull blade dragged through the rind of an orange. Then the skin parted and the yellow fat beneath it gleamed. Blood welled up so fast the cut disappeared.

Ellis screamed. His heel struck the floor twice. His hand caught her wrist, and for a second she thought he meant to pull her away. He was trying to hold her still.

“Sorry,” he gasped.

She almost told him it was all right. There was nothing in the room she could honestly say that about.

When the blade touched something hard, she thought she’d found the bullet. A little white crescent came up in the blood. Bone. She looked away just long enough to see the whiskey bottle tipping on its side, rolling a fraction of a turn, stopping against Ellis’s boot.

“Are you done?” he asked.

“No.”

“Lie, then.”

“Nearly.”

He closed his eyes. She put her hand over the wound. Blood squeezed hot between her fingers, and she leaned harder until he made a high, thin sound she wouldn’t have known was his.

Out on the road an engine slowed. Mara held her breath. It slowed a little more, then picked up speed and went on.

“I can do another minute,” Ellis whispered.

“Okay.”

“You have to tell me when it starts.”

She looked down at him. His eyes were open again, fixed on her face.

“Now,” she said, and began to count.

“You can keep your coat,” the interrogator said.

Mara looked down. She hadn’t realized she was holding it shut with both hands.

“I thought you’d be cold,” he added.

“What time is it?”

“Almost six.”

“You said that before.”

“Yes.”

He set a laptop between them and turned it around. The password field was empty. Behind the login window was a photograph of Mara and her sister on a ferry. Her sister had been seasick that morning. She’d smiled for the picture anyway.

“You could have changed the wallpaper,” Mara said.

“I could have.”

She looked at the door. A few minutes earlier, someone on the other side had asked if he was ready. He’d said, *Give us a minute*, in the same tone she used when a waiter came by before she’d read the menu.

“Are you going to do it?” she asked.

“No.”

The relief came so quickly she hated herself for it.

“I’m going to step outside,” he said. “You’ll still be able to ask for me.”

Mara tucked her hands under her arms. One of her thumbnails had left a little white crescent in the other.

“What if I tell you and you leave anyway?”

“Then you’ll have been wrong about me.”

She laughed once. It sounded like a cough.

“You want me to trust you.”

“I want you to type a password. You don’t have to think well of me afterward.”

He got up. His chair scraped the floor, and Mara flinched. They both looked at the chair.

“Wait,” she said.

He stopped.

She’d meant to follow it with something. A bargain, or a question that would take him a long time to answer. Now that he was standing there, she couldn’t think of anything except that when he opened the door she’d be able to see who was on the other side.

“Could you sit down again?” she asked.

He took his hand off the knob.

Mara put her hands on the keyboard. For a moment, she couldn’t remember the password at all.

The stairwell door wouldn’t open.

Mara pulled until her shoulder gave a little click. Then she let go, counted to three, and pulled again, as if the first time she’d simply done it wrong.

Smoke caught in her throat. She coughed, and the breath she dragged in afterward was worse. She dropped to her knees. Down here she could still see the baseboards, the brass doorstop, the stupid little felt pads she’d put under the hall table so it wouldn’t scratch the floor.

The backs of her hands had begun to blister. She tucked them under her arms without thinking. For one absurd second she wanted her mother, not to save her but to look at her hands and tell her how bad it was.

*You can have the house*, she’d told Adrian that morning. He’d stood on the porch and studied her face until she’d had to look away. Now she understood what he’d been waiting to see.

She crawled toward the bedroom window. Halfway there, the ceiling came down behind her. The floor jumped under her knees, and she screamed with what little air she had left.

Three taps answered from beneath the floorboards.

A pause. Then two more.

It was the knock she and Adrian had used as children, when one of them needed the other to open a door without waking their father.

“Mara,” Adrian said from below. “Don’t move.”

Her palm was already sinking through the floor.

The case looked like it ought to hold a trombone. I’d always liked that about it. A man could carry it through a hotel lobby and people would assume he was about to do something they wouldn’t pay to hear.

Upstairs, I opened it on a towel. I laid out the pieces and took my watch off so the buckle wouldn’t knock against the metal. Then I put the rifle together. There wasn’t much noise. The ice machine down the hall made more of a fuss dropping six cubes into a bucket.

The man in the photograph had a name. The man who paid me had gone to some trouble not to use it.

“He’s hurt a lot of people,” he’d said.

I asked him how many.

He told me how much.

I’d spent the last two days trying to remember whether I’d asked because I cared about the answer or because I wanted him to raise the price.

Across the street, a waiter was setting out glasses on the restaurant terrace. He held each one up to the light before he put it down. One had a spot on it. He polished it with his apron, looked again, and took it back inside. Nobody would ever know he’d done that.

I used to think the money made it different. Not cleaner, exactly. More like the way a receipt makes a bad dinner official. You paid for it, so there must have been a meal.

My client had given me half in advance. I’d used some of it to fix a tooth. For the first time in six months I could drink coffee without it hurting. That was the sort of detail I never put in when I told myself what kind of man I was.

I set the photograph facedown. Then I turned it back over.

I read his name out loud. My voice sounded ordinary. I’d been hoping for something worse.

Nico counted the money twice under the light above the butcher shop’s back door.

“You’re short.”

“By how much?”

The question bothered him more than the missing money. Ray had known exactly what he owed on Tuesday, when he’d called to ask for another day.

“Four hundred.”

“I can get four hundred.”

“Then why’d you come?”

Ray looked down the alley, toward the street. “I thought you might take what I had.”

Nico put the envelope inside his coat. Ray pulled a knife. It was a little folding thing with a yellow handle. Nico had seen him use it to cut an apple into quarters for his daughter.

“Give it back,” Ray said.

Nico caught Ray’s sleeve when he reached for the coat. They hit the butcher’s door together, hard enough to rattle it in its frame. Ray’s heel slipped on a flattened carton. For a second all Nico was doing was holding him up.

Then he felt a hard shove low in his side. It didn’t hurt until he took a breath. The pain came hot and surprisingly deep, and the breath stopped halfway in. He put his hand under his coat. His shirt was warm there, and getting warmer.

Ray let go of him. The knife clicked against the pavement.

“Sit down,” Ray said.

Nico tried. His knees folded before he’d decided where to put his feet. Ray crouched beside him, took out his phone, and dropped it. He picked it up with both hands.

“What’s the address?”

Nico knew the butcher’s name. He knew the man closed early on Thursdays and left a bowl of water out for dogs. He’d been coming down this alley for six years. He couldn’t think of the street number.

“Just tell them it’s the butcher’s,” he said. “They’ll know.”

The rain had stopped ten minutes ago. In the alley it went on falling, off the fire escapes and the sagging awning over the butcher’s back door. Detective Mara Vale stood inside the tape and listened until she could tell the drips apart.

“Anybody move him?”

The young patrolman shook his head. He’d tucked his hands under his arms, though it wasn’t cold enough for that.

The dead man lay on his back beside a stack of milk crates. One heel had caught in the bottom crate and lifted it half an inch off the pavement. His coat was open. The shirt underneath had gone black down the front, except where the rain had washed a narrow stripe pink. There was a broken tooth on his lower lip. Each time a drop struck his cheek, the tooth shifted a little.

Vale crouched. The alley smelled of wet cardboard, old fryer grease, and blood. A kitchen fan rattled in the wall above her, blowing warm air across the body. Somewhere on the other side of the bricks, somebody called for two eggs over easy.

She took out her notebook.

“Who found him?”

“Dishwasher. Came out for a smoke.”

“Where is he?”

“Inside. I told him he could wash his hands.”

Vale looked up. The patrolman swallowed.

“He had blood on them?”

“I didn’t ask.”

“All right. Go sit with him. Don’t ask now.”

She waited for his footsteps to clear the alley before leaning closer. The dead man’s right hand was curled against his chest. There was a faint blue stamp on the back of it, blurred by the rain. She angled her flashlight. A bird, maybe, with a crown over its head. She drew what she could see without touching him.

At the mouth of the alley, a bus knelt at the curb. Its headlights swept over the man’s shoes. The laces on the left one had been replaced with white kitchen string, doubled and knotted neatly. Vale wrote that down, too. People trying to identify a body often couldn’t tell you what color their husband’s eyes were. They could tell you he’d broken a shoelace on Tuesday.

The first thing Martin stuffed into Mr. Bell was a receipt for a birthday cake.

He’d found it in the dead man’s coat. The bakery had misspelled *Eleanor*, and Mr. Bell had drawn a little caret between the missing letters. Martin folded the receipt along that mark and slipped it beneath the waistcoat.

“Something of your own,” he said. He said this to all of them at the beginning.

His collection occupied the front parlor, where the afternoon light was kind. Mrs. Vale stood by the window with her binoculars. The postman sat on the piano bench, one hand hovering over middle C. Martin had killed both of them, and seven others besides, but it embarrassed him to think of that part of the work. It was like remembering what he’d said as a boy when he wanted someone to look at him.

He packed the rest of Mr. Bell with the things he’d collected over six weeks: the paper sleeve from a railway sandwich, a glove worn thin at the thumb, the losing half of a raffle ticket. He tucked a wool sock into each shoulder of the jacket until the slope looked right. Then he stepped back.

The hands were wrong. Martin had arranged them on the knees, but in every photograph Mr. Bell had one hand in a pocket. He tried the right pocket first, then the left. The left was better. It made him look as if he were waiting outside a shop, willing to be patient for another minute or two.

While Martin was adjusting the cuff, something crinkled beneath the waistcoat.

“Dad?” said a little girl.

Martin let go of the sleeve.

“Dad, they spelled it wrong again.”

The voice came from the receipt. He knew it with the same certainty with which he knew, when the telephone rang at a certain hour, that it was his sister.

He reached for the waistcoat buttons. Mr. Bell’s hand came out of his pocket and closed around Martin’s wrist.

Across the room, the postman lowered his finger onto middle C. The piano was a little flat. Martin had been meaning to have it tuned.

One by one, his collection began to take things out of their pockets. Mrs. Vale unfolded a bus timetable. The postman took out a key. A woman Martin had never found a name for shook a handful of beach sand onto his good rug.

Mr. Bell rose. One of the socks dropped out of his jacket. He looked down at it and gave a brief, apologetic smile, and Martin had the awful feeling that this was the first expression he’d ever seen on the man’s face that he hadn’t put there himself.

They left by the front door. Nobody looked back.

Martin went from room to room, collecting what he could find of himself. There was a photograph in which he’d been cut in half to fit the frame. There was a birthday card from his sister, signed *Love*, with nothing underneath. At the bottom of the kitchen drawer he found a shopping list in his own handwriting.

He carried these things to the parlor and sat in Mr. Bell’s chair. He put the photograph and the card inside his coat. The shopping list he kept in his hand.

He waited for one of them to speak.

After a while he unfolded the list. He had written *milk* twice.

On the ninth morning, Mara caught herself thinking of Daniel as food.

Not his body. Daniel. The distinction had held for two days, and when it failed, nothing happened. The fuselage creaked as the sun reached it. Across from her, Ellis was trying to get his swollen foot back into his boot.

“Leave it off,” she said. “You’ll never get it off again.”

Ellis left it off.

She had loved Daniel in the ordinary way you come to love a stranger when you’re both waiting to die. He’d known how to make her laugh without making her ribs hurt. He’d told her about a fight with his daughter over a missing Tupperware lid, and how he’d found the lid the morning of the flight and left it on the counter without saying anything. The daughter would come home and find it. Mara had been thinking about that for two days.

Now Ellis held out a scrap of foil. She took it because his hand was shaking, and for a moment that was all she was doing: taking something from someone who might drop it.

She tried to think of her son. She’d meant to say his name before she ate, to make it clear to herself what she was doing and why. But she was afraid that if she thought of him now, she wouldn’t be able to put the food in her mouth.

So she looked at the boot beside Ellis’s foot and took the bite.

The first chew was deliberate. The second wasn’t. She’d expected to have to fight herself all the way through it, but her mouth knew what to do, and then she swallowed.

Ellis looked down at the foil. Mara thought he was asking for it back. When she held it out to him, she saw that she’d already folded it shut to save the rest for later.

The worst part was that the bowl was warm.

Daniel had hoped for cold. Cold would have made it feel like something from the back of a refrigerator, something he could swallow before his mouth figured out what it was. But the bowl had been sitting under a lamp. The pale grubs moved slowly in the heat, folding over one another in a shallow pool of brown liquid.

The speaker clicked. “You have forty seconds.”

He picked up the spoon. It rattled against his teeth, though he hadn’t meant to bring it that close yet.

On the other side of the glass, his brother kept his eyes on Daniel’s face. He’d been watching the bowl until Daniel asked him not to.

Daniel pinched his nose and shoved the spoon into his mouth.

For half a second there was only the taste of metal. Then something burst against the roof of his mouth. It tasted like the water at the bottom of a vase after the flowers had died. He gagged so hard his heels lifted off the floor. The spoon clattered away.

“Look at me,” his brother said.

Daniel did. His eyes were watering too badly to make out much besides the blue of his brother’s shirt. He’d borrowed that shirt last Christmas and spilled gravy on the cuff. His brother had said it didn’t matter, then gone right upstairs to wash it.

He tried to swallow. His throat closed, opened, closed again. A little of the liquid went down the wrong way. He coughed through his nose, terrified that if he opened his mouth even a fraction, he’d lose what he’d managed to get down and have to do it all again.

Then the last soft lump passed.

The display stopped at three seconds. Somewhere behind the glass, a lock clicked.

Daniel pressed the back of his hand to his mouth. He could still feel something moving against his gums. He knew it was only his tongue, checking.

He couldn’t make it stop.

Detective Vale found the note beneath the rabbit’s water bowl. A wet crescent had softened one corner. The rest of the paper was clean, torn from a school exercise book along the perforations.

At the top, in purple pencil, someone had written **WHY I HAD TO**. The *I* had been erased and written again, smaller.

> Mom said that if I ever wanted to hurt something, I should tell her.
>
> I told her on Tuesday. She said everybody gets angry.
>
> I wasn’t angry. I told her that part twice.
>
> I picked Button because I loved him. I thought if I picked something I didn’t love, it wouldn’t tell me anything.
>
> I said his name first. He came over. I thought when he did that I would change my mind.
>
> That’s why I had to. I needed to know if there was a part of me that would stop me even if nobody came in.
>
> There isn’t. Please tell Mom I answered her question.

Vale read the last line again.

In the kitchen, the boy’s mother sat at the table in her slippers. She had set out a juice box for him before the officers arrived. The straw was still in its wrapper.

“What question did you ask him?” Vale said.

The woman looked up. “When?”

“Tuesday.”

For a while the only sound was the refrigerator.

“I asked him if he thought I had to watch him every minute.” She touched the straw with one fingertip. “I wasn’t really asking.”

The first skin came off in the shower. Nora rubbed her thumb over a pale patch on her wrist and felt the whole palm slip loose. It lay in the drain like a glove turned inside out, with the little crescent scar she’d gotten opening a tin of peaches at nine. By Friday, the skin beneath had grown too ridged to leave a fingerprint.

The bones changed at night. One rib would break, then another, and she’d lie still while the ends grated past each other and joined again at a steeper angle. In the morning she could measure the change by which buttons still closed on her nightgown. Her jaw was worse. It broke while she was on the phone with her sister. She managed to say *dropped my mug* before the second crack, and her sister, who had heard the first one, asked if she’d cut her feet.

For a while, Nora kept a list of things not to do. Don’t follow people home. Don’t stand outside the nursery window. Take Mrs. Vale’s groceries upstairs even if she calls you by your mother’s name.

The last one held longest. On Tuesday, Nora carried up two bags and put the milk away because Mrs. Vale’s hands were bad. Then she went down to the lobby and took the old woman’s name off the buzzer.

She used to do kind things without thinking. It was disconcerting how long the habit lasted after she’d stopped caring.

The first shovelful landed above Mara’s face.

She knew it was dirt because she could hear the clods break apart. A heavy smack, a scatter of smaller sounds, and then one pebble rolling down the lid until it lodged somewhere near her left ear.

She opened her mouth to call out and hit her front teeth on the wood.

For a moment that was all she could think about: she hadn’t even opened her mouth all the way.

“Wait,” she said.

Another shovelful. She got her palms flat against the lid, but there was no room to get her elbows beneath them. She pushed anyway. Her wrists bent back. The lid didn’t move.

“Wait!”

They had to stop between shovelfuls. There had to be time to put the shovel back in the pile. She listened for that gap and tried to fit a scream into it, but she came in too early and heard the dirt strike through the middle of her own voice.

She tried to take a slow breath. The air was warm now. She could smell the pine and the sourness of her own breath, and there was no direction she could turn her head to get away from either. She tucked her chin, trying to make a little more room for her chest. It worked just enough that she did it again, though there was nowhere left for her chin to go.

The dirt sounded different. It no longer rattled on the wood. Each load fell softly onto the one before it, and she began to dread the softness more than she’d dreaded the blows.

Then it stopped.

Mara held still. Someone up there might be holding still too, one hand on the shovel, listening.

She had enough air to call once more. She waited for a footstep, for the scrape of a boot, for any hint of where to aim her voice.

The breath slipped out of her while she waited.

The first thing the surgeons took from Mara was the ability to close her eyes.

She learned this when the light came on. She tried to blink and felt the effort travel as far as her temples, where it stopped. A nurse leaned over her and put a drop of water in each eye. The water ran into her ears.

“Can you tell us your name?” the nurse asked.

“Mara Vale.”

The nurse turned to somebody Mara couldn’t see. “Speech is still voluntary.”

For a while the pain had places. There was the hot line beneath her ribs and the deep, blunt pressure in her left hip. Then something under the table began to pull, and she couldn’t have said where it hurt. She tried to get away from the pain and found that there was nowhere inside herself it hadn’t already reached. Her right hand opened on the sheet. She hadn’t opened it.

“Good,” somebody said.

She’d promised her son she would come home with milk. This was the thought she kept returning to, even after she understood that she wasn’t going home. She could see him standing on the bottom shelf of the refrigerator to reach the carton, though she’d told him a dozen times not to. She tried to say his name while she still could.

“Repeat,” said the nurse.

“Eli,” Mara said.

“Ready,” said her mouth a moment later, in the same breath.

On her first shift, she stood in a trench beneath the municipal laundry and turned a wheel. The wheel was stiff at the top of each turn. Her shoulder hurt when she reached that point, and after a while she began to dread it on the way up. She could still dread things. Nobody had needed to take that out.

Once, a woman sorting sheets above the trench dropped a sock. It was small and yellow, with a gray heel. Mara knew the way a child’s foot would feel through it. She tried to take one hand off the wheel.

The woman glanced down. “Leave it,” she told her coworker. “It can’t pick things up.”

Mara wanted to tell her that she knew that. She wanted to ask her to pick it up anyway. But her mouth had been given only one thing to say when someone spoke to her at work.

“Ready,” she said, and her shoulder came around again.

The first time Mara Vale called a crime scene beautiful, she was alone in a laundry room, and the word escaped her on an exhale.

After that, she was careful to say *orderly*.

Orderly was a word you could put in a report. It described the row of shoes beneath a dead man’s bed, the unopened mail sorted by size. Beautiful was what she meant when she took the long way home so she could pass a house where something terrible had happened and see whether the upstairs light still came on at dusk.

She began carrying two notebooks. In the department-issued one she wrote measurements, times, the names of those present. In the other she drew. Never the bodies, at first. Just the space around them.

Then came the woman in the conservatory.

It was January. The house had been without heat for three days, and ice had feathered the glass from the corners inward, leaving a clear oval in each pane. Through those ovals Mara could see pieces of the garden: a black branch, a yellow hose, a stone rabbit with one ear. None of the pieces joined up.

The woman lay on her side among the potted citrus trees, wearing a blue housecoat. One slipper was gone. Above her, a lemon hung so low that its tip almost touched her shoulder.

Mara stopped in the doorway.

At first she thought the killer had cut the flowers. White petals lay in a crescent along the woman’s back, bright against the blue. Then she saw the small bare stems above them. The cold had done it. The cold had also clouded the glass and turned the soil in the pots the dark, flat color of bakers’ chocolate. Outside, a passing car sent a band of light through the clear ovals. One after another, the pots flashed green.

The woman’s bare heel was cracked. She had mended the cuff of her housecoat with thread a shade too dark.

Mara would remember that cuff long after she forgot the wound.

“Need another minute?” asked Ellis, behind her.

She did. She wanted the car to pass again. She wanted to see if the green would be the same.

“No,” she said, and stepped aside.

The woman’s name was Ruth Ansel. Her daughter came in the next morning wearing two different socks. She’d dressed in the dark so as not to wake her children, she explained, though nobody had asked.

“Were the trees all right?” she said.

Mara told her about the cold.

“Oh,” the daughter said. She pressed her thumbs together. “She used to call me when they flowered. She’d hold the phone up to them. I kept telling her I couldn’t smell them over the phone.”

She laughed once, and then she asked about her mother.

That night, Mara opened the second notebook. She’d drawn the conservatory from the doorway, with the pots and the windowpanes and the hollow curve of the blue housecoat. She had even drawn the petals. In the lower corner, where an artist might sign her name, she had written the time.

She turned the page and tried to draw Ruth Ansel holding a telephone up to a flowering tree. She didn’t know how Ruth had worn her hair when she was alive. The first thing Owen recognized was a mitten.

It was blue, with a white rabbit stitched on the thumb. He’d seen it on the missing poster at the bus stop, in a photograph of a woman holding up both hands to show off what she’d knitted. In the picture the rabbit looked like it was waving.

The mitten lay on a shelf in his neighbor’s basement, beneath a little brass plate engraved with the woman’s name.

Owen had come over to shut off the water. Frank was away for the weekend, and a pipe had burst in the cold. *You’ve got a key,* Frank had said over the phone. *Valve’s at the bottom of the stairs. Thanks, pal.*

At the bottom of the stairs, water was running under a door. The wood had swollen around the latch. Owen had put his shoulder into it, thinking about the Persian rug upstairs, which Frank always asked him not to step on with his shoes.

Now he stood with one wet shoe inside the room.

There were nineteen brass plates. Owen counted them twice because counting was something he could do without having to look too closely at what sat above them. A pair of glasses, one lens starred with a crack. A heel worn down on the outside. A wallet with a grocery list sticking out of it. Beside the wallet, on a white saucer, lay two front teeth. A shred of gray gum still joined them at the roots.

He looked away and saw the jars.

In the nearest one, a severed hand rested palm up in cloudy liquid. The skin had swollen around a wedding band until only a thin edge of gold showed. In the next jar was an ear with a pearl stud in it. The flesh had gone the color of cooked egg white; the pearl still looked pretty. Behind the jars, pinned flat to a square of cork, was a patch of tattooed skin. Its edges had dried and curled inward, taking the last two letters of *MOM* with them.

Owen smelled the room only after he saw all this. Under the wet plaster and the sharp chemical sting was a faint sweetness, like the juice at the bottom of a garbage bag. He swallowed and felt his throat close around nothing.

Then he saw the knitting needle.

It was tucked into the blue mitten. Owen could see its blunt silver end at the cuff. He remembered the missing woman’s sister on the local news saying she kept hoping her sister would walk through the door so she could tell her the stupid mittens didn’t match. The rabbits both faced the same way.

Owen backed into the doorframe. His phone slipped out of his wet hand and struck the concrete. It lit up where it landed.

**FRANK:** Did you find it?

He bent to pick up the phone. From down there he could see beneath the lowest shelf, where the rising water had reached a row of cardboard boxes. On the nearest box was a photograph of his own front porch. He was in it, sitting on the step in his socks, holding a coffee mug between his knees.

Frank had brought him that coffee the morning after his wife left. Owen remembered how grateful he’d been that Frank hadn’t asked him to talk.

The phone vibrated again.

**FRANK:** The valve, I mean.

Owen went up the stairs without turning off the water. Outside, he crossed the street to the Garcias’ and knocked until Mrs. Garcia opened the door. He asked her to call the police. Then he asked if he could come inside.

She looked down at his feet. He’d left one shoe in the basement. He had no idea when.

“Of course,” she said, and opened the door wider.

The first thing to rise was the smell.

It came up through the snow, sweet and close, like apples left to rot in a shut room. Then the snow sagged. A hand pushed through it, the wool of its mitten stitched to the wrist by a winter’s worth of ice. When the hand closed, the mitten split. Two of the fingers were down to bone.

At the foot of the hill, the necromancer rang his bell a second time.

Mara heard it stop. That was the sound it made: not a note, but the abrupt end of one. Her ears strained after the missing sound until her jaw ached. Beneath her boots, the ground began to move.

The dead had been buried in ranks because there hadn’t been time to dig individual graves. They rose in ranks, too. A spearman came up with his cheek pressed to the back of the man ahead of him. When they pulled apart, a strip of his face stayed on the other man’s coat. A woman in an officer’s sash put a hand to her belly as she stood. The hand went in nearly to the wrist. She withdrew it, smoothed the sash, and stood at attention.

The necromancer spoke.

All along the hillside, snow slipped off shoulders and flew upward into the dark. Mara watched a flake rise past her eye, whole and sharp, though she had felt it melt on her cheek a moment before.

Then she heard her brother take a breath.

She knew it by the little catch at the end. He’d breathed like that since a horse kicked him in the ribs at twelve. She’d sat beside his bed and listened to it for six nights. She’d listened for it again when they brought him home from the pass, and in the awful quiet she’d put her ear right against his mouth.

Now he stood in the third rank, his lips still sewn together with her blue thread.

The necromancer turned toward the road. A thousand dead soldiers turned with him.

Only her brother hesitated. He lifted one hand, palm out, the way he used to at the bend in the road when he knew she was still watching from the house.

Then the bell stopped again, and he put his hand down.

My brother was telling me how to prune the pear tree when his fork slipped.

It struck the edge of his plate and fell into his lap. He looked down, annoyed, as though the fork had interrupted him on purpose.

“Above the bud,” he said. “You cut just above it. Otherwise you get that dead bit sticking out.”

“I remember.”

“You always say that.”

He retrieved the fork and wiped it on his napkin. By the time he set it down, the tines were ticking against the plate.

I had imagined I would know when the poison began to work. In the kitchen, with the door shut, I’d pictured a clean division: one moment he would be eating dinner and the next he would be dying. Instead there was my brother putting his left hand over his right to still it, and both of us pretending that I hadn’t noticed.

“Is it hot in here?” he asked.

“No.”

He loosened his collar anyway. His face had gone pale around the mouth, and a bead of sweat ran from his temple into his sideburn. He reached for his water. The rim clicked against his teeth.

“Do you want me to open a window?”

“Finish your dinner,” he said. “I’m all right.”

It was what he used to say when he took me out for lunch as a child and ate slowly so I wouldn’t see that he’d bought himself less. Until that moment I’d managed, for nearly six months, to remember only the things I needed to remember about him.

He tried to sit back. His shoulders missed the chair, and he caught himself on the table with both hands. The candle flame tipped in the draft from his sleeve. He stared at it, breathing fast now, his mouth open.

“Something’s wrong,” he said.

I got up. He reached for my wrist with such relief that I understood he still thought I was the person who would help him.

In the hall I picked up the telephone. I could hear him shifting in his chair, trying like a guest to make as little noise as possible. Then a shoe scraped hard against the floor.

The operator asked me what had happened.

“My brother’s ill,” I said.

From the dining room he called my name. He got the first syllable out, and then, after a breath, tried it again.

“I poisoned him,” I said, and gave her the address.

The carpenter had left a nail sticking up at the end of the plank. Every time the ship rolled, it caught in the hem of Jonah Vale’s trousers.

“Captain,” he said.

Mara Venn waited. She had sailed with Jonah for eleven years. He had called her Mara through two hurricanes and a winter in a Spanish prison. Last night, when he came into her cabin with a pistol, he had called her Mara then, too.

“Tell them it was only me.”

“You brought six men to my door.”

“Aye,” he said. “But I told them you were already dead.”

Below him, a shark turned on its side. Its pale belly caught the last of the light. Jonah looked back at the deck, where the six men stood unbound among the rest of the crew. Not one could meet his eye.

The ship rolled. Jonah’s hem caught again. He bent by instinct to free it, and for a moment he was just a man stooping over a snag in his trousers. Then the plank rose beneath him and he went off sideways.

He surfaced with a gasp and struck out for the ship. He was a good swimmer. Mara remembered that too late to stop herself from looking for the rope ladder. Someone had hauled it in.

The first shark caught him by the calf. He jerked upright in the water and screamed. When his leg came free, the foot hung at an angle and strips of white cloth trailed from the wound. He kept swimming. He made two more strokes before a second shark struck him under the ribs and rolled him over. His back broke the surface, his hands scrabbling at the animal’s slick flank. Then the water churned white and red, and a torn sleeve floated clear with nothing in it.

No one cheered. At the rail, one of the six men opened his mouth and drew a breath so sharp Mara heard it over the slap of the waves.

“Get that plank in,” she said.

The carpenter hauled it aboard. There was a scrap of Jonah’s trouser leg on the nail. He picked it off carefully, folded it once, and put it in his pocket.

The first time Nora heard Eli after she killed him, he was in the hallway, emptying his pockets.

Keys in the dish. Loose change. Then the little pause while he hooked his thumb through his wedding ring and pulled it off. He always took it off to wash the dishes. He was afraid it would slip down the drain.

Nora lay perfectly still in bed.

“Nora,” he called. “Have you eaten?”

She bit the inside of her cheek until she tasted blood. He had asked her that the night she killed him. She had said no. There was a plate for her in the oven when the police came, with another plate inverted over it to keep the food warm.

In the morning, the dish in the hall was empty.

For a while she could tell which things weren’t real. Eli’s reflection in the kitchen window didn’t move when she turned the tap off. The voice that said *excuse me* from behind her in the grocery store came from a woman reaching for a tin of peaches, though Nora heard it in Eli’s voice and felt his hand, distinctly, at the small of her back.

She began leaving herself notes.

**THE TAPPING IS THE RADIATOR.**

**YOU PUT THAT CUP THERE.**

**THERE IS NO ONE IN THE BATH.**

She found the last one stuck to the bathroom door one morning. It was in her handwriting. She didn’t remember writing it. From the other side came the soft squeak of a bare heel against porcelain.

She went to work without brushing her teeth.

By the end of the month she was sleeping at the kitchen table. She couldn’t bear the bedroom, where the mattress still sloped gently toward his side. She started making his coffee in the mornings. The first time, she poured it away. The second time, she left it until evening, and when she came home there was a pale crescent at the bottom of the cup where he hadn’t quite finished it.

She called his mother.

“I need to tell you something,” Nora said.

“Oh, love,” his mother said, and began to cry.

Nora listened to her cry. Then she said she was sorry she hadn’t called sooner, and hung up.

That night Eli sat across from her at the kitchen table. She could see the faint dent in his hair where he’d worn his headphones. One of his socks had a hole at the heel. She had promised to throw those socks out.

“I know,” she told him. “I know what I did.”

He turned his coffee cup so the handle faced her. He’d always done that when he made her a drink.

“I can tell them,” she said.

Eli waited.

She picked up the phone. When the dispatcher asked what had happened, Nora looked at him. He was rubbing a spot on the table with his thumb. A little dried coffee. She could hear his thumbnail catch on it.

“My husband is here,” she said.

“Is he threatening you?”

“No.”

At noon the trams stopped running. The government had discovered that people were more willing to attend an execution if there was no way to get across town until it was over.

Attendance in the square was voluntary. The clerks at its four entrances stamped your work card to prove you had volunteered.

Mara stood beside the woman who had reported the theft. She knew her from the bakery, where the woman always slipped a second roll into the bag if you came just before closing. Today she held a paper parcel against her chest.

“Is that it?” Mara asked.

The woman nodded. The court had returned the loaf that morning. It was too stale to sell.

On the platform, a magistrate read the boy’s name, his age, and the price of the bread. At sixteen, Emil Venn was old enough to be sentenced as a man but, by law, too young to be named in the newspapers. Tomorrow’s account would call him *a youth*.

He found somebody in the crowd and lifted his chin. A girl near the fountain lifted hers back. It had the quick, embarrassed look of a greeting exchanged in a school corridor.

The magistrate asked if he had anything to say.

“Did my sister get here?”

The girl by the fountain opened her mouth. The man beside her took her hand. He didn’t pull her back or put a finger to his lips. He just held on, and whatever she had meant to say came out as a breath.

A woman in the front row began to clap when the magistrate closed his book. She stopped after three sharp beats. It was the wrong moment. The crowd had been taught to applaud afterward.

When the trap fell, Mara heard someone behind her say, “Oh,” in the rueful tone people used when a cup slipped off a table. The applause started by the west gate and spread unevenly. A man clapped with his gloves still tucked under his arm; one fell, and he left it where it landed. A little boy clapped hard until his father caught both his wrists.

The baker hadn’t moved. People had to turn sideways to get past her as the square emptied. At last she went to the girl by the fountain and held out the parcel.

The girl took it. For a moment Mara thought she might throw it down. Instead she tucked it under her coat.

“Is there a knife at home?” the man beside her asked.

The girl shook her head.

“All right,” he said. “We’ll soak it.”

The tram bells rang. The three of them stood at the curb, waiting for the first one to come.

The woman stopped when the forest stopped.

A moment earlier, rain had been ticking through the leaves in a thousand small, separate sounds. Then the wind dropped, and she stood with one foot raised above the path, listening.

He waited for her to put it down.

“Hello?” she said.

How polite people were, even here. She said it the way someone might answer a knock at the door, a little annoyed at having to get up. He wondered if she heard that in her own voice. Probably not. She was already holding her breath again.

For years he had told himself he liked the fear. Fear was easy to name. But it was this he came for: the interval after *hello*, when somebody still believed the world owed them an answer.

Her foot came down in the mud.

“Come on, Rachel,” she whispered.

That caught him off guard. He had spent the better part of an hour thinking of her as the woman in the red coat. Now, in a voice so ordinary she might have been trying to get herself out of bed on a cold morning, she had given herself a name.

He wished she hadn’t.

She started walking again. Somewhere water ran beneath the trail, and when she crossed the little wooden bridge her steps rang out, quick and hollow. On the other side she broke into a run. A branch caught her hood and pulled it back. She let out a small, furious sound, almost a word.

He followed.

What he loved, if he was honest, was being waited for. In the rest of his life he could leave a room and come back twenty minutes later to find that nobody had noticed. Out here, this stranger had stopped in the rain and asked him to speak. She had wanted to hear his voice more than she had wanted anything in the world.

It was a shabby sort of pleasure once he put it into words. He tried not to.

Ahead, a light came on.

Not a flashlight. A square of yellow between the trunks, with a white curtain hanging crooked across it. Rachel saw it a second after he did. She called out, and her voice cracked on the first syllable. She called again.

A dog barked. He heard a chair scrape across a floor.

“You all right out there?” a man called.

“No,” Rachel said.

She sounded astonished. Then she said it again, louder, and began to cry.

The door opened. He could see the man in the rectangle of light, barefoot, one hand reaching back inside to keep the dog from getting out. Rachel was telling him something in short bursts. Twice she looked over her shoulder. The third time, she didn’t.

He stayed among the trees until the man shut the door. Through the crooked curtain he could see the shadow of the dog going back and forth as someone talked to it, low and patient, until it settled.

Officer Vale waited until Mrs. Alvarez went back into her apartment. She had offered him coffee twice, once when he arrived and again when he told her there’d been a death downstairs. He’d remember that when he took her statement. A woman who offered coffee at a time like that could be persuaded she’d been too upset to hear what she’d heard.

Across the hall, Noah Bell’s door stood open. Noah himself was sitting in the back of a patrol car in his socks. He’d come downstairs when he heard the shot and tried to stop the bleeding with a dish towel. There was blood on both his sleeves.

Vale stepped inside.

On the kitchen table lay a crossword with one answer rubbed out so hard the paper had torn. Beside it, a mug held three pencils, all sharpened. Vale had expected a mess. In a mess you could set something down anywhere and it would belong.

He opened the cutlery drawer. Everything had its slot, even the little fork people kept for no reason. He closed it again.

From the street came the brief squawk of a radio. He had perhaps a minute before Dwyer came up. Dwyer would look wherever Vale was looking, then a little farther. She was a good officer. He’d asked for her by name because when she testified she never claimed to remember anything she didn’t.

There was a coat over the back of a chair. Vale put the dead man’s wallet in its pocket.

He’d taken it because his own photograph was inside. He’d meant to leave the wallet on the body, but after he took out the photograph he’d heard Noah’s bare feet on the stairs. For the last twenty minutes that ordinary black wallet had been the most dangerous thing in the city. Now it was a reason for Noah Bell to have gone downstairs.

Not a very good reason. The wallet held eleven dollars.

But the prosecutor wouldn’t have to say Noah had killed for eleven dollars. She could say he hadn’t known how much was in it.

“Vale?” Dwyer called from the landing.

“Kitchen.”

She stopped in the doorway. “Kid wants to know if someone can bring him his shoes.”

Vale looked down. There they were under the chair, the laces still tied. He could picture Noah pushing his feet into them every morning without undoing the knots. No reason to picture that. He picked up the shoes.

“Sure,” he said. “Check his coat while you’re here. He’ll be cold.”

At seven in the morning on the third of November, 1824, Edmund Vale apologized for keeping the other gentlemen waiting. The ferry had been slow, he said. Nobody mentioned that he had come on foot.

His sister had asked him the night before what would happen if he simply stayed home. He had told her that she did not understand these things. Now, in a wet pasture outside Calais, watching his second try to scrape the mud from a borrowed boot, he wished he had given her question the courtesy of an answer.

Across the field, Lieutenant Harcourt took off his spectacles and handed them to the surgeon. Without them he looked younger, and Edmund remembered that he was.

They fired almost together.

Edmund saw a twig fall from the hedge behind Harcourt. Then he sat down. He had not decided to sit; the ground was simply there, cold through his trousers, and both his hands were pressed to his stomach.

The surgeon knelt beside him and asked him to move his hands. Edmund tried. The pain was so much worse when he let go that he seized the surgeon’s wrist and begged him, quite politely at first, to stop.

“Very well,” the surgeon said, and laid his coat over Edmund’s legs.

For the first two minutes Edmund kept thinking the worst of the pain must have passed. Each time it eased he drew a breath, and each breath set it going again. He tried to find a position in which he could bear it. There was none. Finally he asked his second, a man he had known since school, to hold him still. His friend did so, though afterward he could not remember putting his arms around him.

Harcourt came near enough to cast a shadow.

“Was it you who told her?” Edmund asked.

Harcourt bent down. “Told whom?”

“My sister. About today.”

“No.”

Edmund shut his eyes. He had been angry with her for asking him to stay. He could remember the exact care with which she had buttered a piece of toast while he explained why he couldn’t.

The church bell began to ring. Edmund had heard it every morning that week without ever counting the strokes. Now he counted four, lost the fifth when the pain caught him, and asked whether it had stopped. His friend said yes, although it was still ringing.

By the time the bell fell quiet, Edmund had stopped asking to be moved. He wanted his friend to loosen his collar, then to fasten it again because he was cold. A minute or two later he began to say his sister’s name. His friend leaned closer, expecting a message, but Edmund only said it once more.

Harcourt had been holding the surgeon’s watch. At last the surgeon took it back from him and closed the case. Nine minutes had passed since the shots.

In the account they sent to England, the two seconds agreed that Mr. Vale had borne his wound with extraordinary composure. His friend wrote that sentence twice. The first time he had written, *He called for you*, and he could not bear to leave it there.

Blood had soaked through the motel towel and into the bedspread, turning the little gold flowers brown. When Mara shifted her weight, a fresh line of red ran down the inside of her knee. She watched it reach the cuff of her sock. That seemed worse, somehow, than the blood on the towel. She’d put on clean socks that morning.

On the nightstand lay a pair of eyebrow tweezers, nail scissors from a drugstore manicure kit, and a steak knife she’d taken from the diner across the road. A grain of dried ketchup clung to the knife handle. She’d meant to scrape it off. Now she couldn’t remember why that had seemed worth doing.

The pain came so fast she didn’t hear herself cry out. She heard the tweezers hit the tile, though: a small, bright sound. Then she was on her side with her cheek against the bedspread, trying to breathe without moving her leg. Even the pull of a breath seemed to reach all the way down into the wound.

Someone knocked on the wall. Once, then twice, harder.

“Sorry,” Mara said. It was the first word she’d managed in ten minutes. She pressed the wet towel to her thigh and tried again, louder this time.

“Help.”

The first thing Rinaldi did was ask if Daniel’s mother still took her coffee with condensed milk.

“She says she doesn’t,” Daniel said.

“She says a lot of things to you, I imagine.”

On the table between them stood two cups of coffee. A third waited on the windowsill, where a pale skin had formed on its surface.

Rinaldi opened a blue folder. “You told the police the shipment came in on Thursday. You told me there was no shipment.”

Daniel had spent six years keeping the two halves of his life apart. He’d imagined that when they came together there would be shouting. Instead, Rinaldi sounded like a man trying to reconcile a pair of invoices before he went home.

“Who else knows?” Rinaldi asked.

“No one.”

The man behind Daniel took his left hand. Daniel turned to look at him and got as far as a white shirt cuff. Then pain went up his arm so fast he felt it in his teeth before he knew what had happened. He heard his chair legs batter the floor. One of his shoes came off.

When the man let go, the nail was lying on the table.

Daniel tried to pull his hand into his lap. Even the air hurt. The pain settled into a pulse, each beat distinct enough to count, and for several seconds counting was the only thing he knew how to do.

Rinaldi pushed a clean napkin toward him. Daniel couldn’t make his good hand pick it up.

“Who else knows?”

“Marin,” Daniel said.

Rinaldi turned a page. “Marin’s been dead since Tuesday.”

Daniel looked at the third cup. He’d been afraid it was for his mother. Now he remembered that Marin always asked for coffee and forgot to drink it.

“You were going to bring him here,” he said.

“He was going to bring you.”

For the first time that night, Rinaldi looked tired. He took a sip, grimaced at the cold coffee, and put it back down.

“Your mother thinks you’re coming for breakfast,” he said. “She asked me to remind you to bring bread.”

Daniel closed his eyes. He could see her at the kitchen table, pinching the corners of yesterday’s paper together so the crumbs wouldn’t fall. He’d always thought that if anything happened to him, she’d have the good sense to leave the city. Now he understood she would wait at that table until somebody came to tell her why he was late.

When the man behind him reached for his hand again, Daniel gave Rinaldi the last name he had. He pronounced it carefully. He didn’t think he could bear to be asked to repeat it.
